blocks.response_text: At 16:52 [reported] lightning struck the Eaton Socon – Wymondley Main circuit 4.5 km [reported] from Wymondley substation. The middle conductor (blue phase) faulted to the earthed transmission tower.
The fault currents were 21 kA [reported] at Wymondley Main and 7 kA [reported] at Eaton Socon, and the blue phase voltage was reduced by approximately 50% [reported].

The main protection at Wymondley Main operated in 70 ms [reported] and at Eaton Socon in 74 ms [reported], clearing the fault within the 80 ms [reported] the Grid Code requires at 400 kV (Connection Condition CC.6.2.3.1.1). Both circuit breakers operated as designed.

The Delayed Auto-Reclose system was available and in service on the circuit and returned it to service within 20 seconds [reported]. That restored the network to the configuration it had before the event and needed no further operational intervention or immediate site attendance.

MeteoGroup's recorded lightning activity near the circuit aligns with our protection data placing the fault 4.5 km [reported] from Wymondley Main, just outside Letchworth Garden City. One of the strikes is timed at the same time as the fault, so we can be confident that a lightning strike was the cause of the fault.

A voltage depression of circa 50% [reported] at the fault location lasted 100 ms [reported]; further from the fault, dips of 20% [reported] lasting 80 ms [reported] were seen. Our monitor at Ryhall recorded a 44% [reported] depression on the blue phase and the one at Necton 21% [reported]. The monitor near Killingholme was unavailable because the Killingholme – Keadby circuit was out of service for planned maintenance.

Engineers attended Wymondley Main and Eaton Socon substations to collect data, including protection operating data; all assets were operating as normal and no defects were identified. Our overhead line engineers inspected the line on the morning of Saturday 10 August and observed no defects.

As is standard practice, the ESO's control room led the response. Our TNCC received electronic alarm indications that the LFDD scheme had operated and confirmed this by phone with the ENCC and DNOs over a period of 8 minutes [reported] after the first indications. Members of the public who rang our safety number were redirected to the 105 number.

Our key finding is that the transmission network operated as designed and in line with standards. Pre-fault and post-fault steady state voltages were within the limits required by industry standards, and harmonic and negative phase sequence currents were within limits.
